(CNN) -- Watch out! Lock up your loved ones! Another bloated, over-produced, high-concept monstrosity has escaped from the labs at Dreamworks Animation, and it's out to devour your kids. Susan, aka "Ginormica," has to save the world in "Monsters vs. Aliens." But don't be too alarmed. "Monsters vs. Aliens" is relatively harmless -- a toothless satire with a knee-jerk feminist theme and a sorry excuse for a plot. That sounds harsh, I know. Who doesn't want to see a 50-foot woman careening through San Francisco on skates that turn out to be automobiles -- the ultimate demolition roller derby? But think about that, just for a second. Roller skates work because they have fixed wheels. Try it with motorcars and you won't get very far. Is that too picky? Perhaps, but you wouldn't find Pixar playing so fast and loose with the laws of physics, and that kind of inattention to detail is typical of the lackadaisical storytelling here and in other Dreamworks animated features. (The talent pool for this one includes the directors of "Shrek 2" and "Shark Tale" and the writers of "Kung Fu Panda" and "The Rocker," incidentally.) High concepts, top-notch voice talent and scattershot pop cultural references are no compensation for a coherent script. The XXXL lady in question -- dubbed "Ginormica" by her U.S. military guards -- starts out plain and petite Susan Murphy (voiced by Reese Witherspoon), until a meteorite hits her just minutes before she's supposed to tie the knot with unctuous chauvinist Derek (Paul Rudd). Her rapid growth spurt saves her from that particular fate worse than death, even if at first glance her new roommates don't look like much of an improvement. There's Dr. Cockroach (Hugh Laurie), a mad scientist who semi-advertently mutated with a bug; B.O.B. (Seth Rogen) an amorphous blue jelly-like blob who gets on just fine without a brain; Missing Link (Will Arnett), a gung-ho amphibian who's all mouth; and a giant dust mite called Insectosaurus who isn't voiced by anyone because he doesn't have anything to say. Sci-fi fans will have fun counting off the references to myriad classics -- "Close Encounters of the Third Kind," "Invaders from Mars," "The Fly," "The Creature from the Black Lagoon," "The Blob," "Mothra" and "Attack of the 50-Foot Woman," for starters -- and noting a few clever bits and pieces (Kiefer Sutherland, as General W.R. Monger, riffs on George C. Scott in "Dr. Strangelove"). The trouble is, once the introductions are over, the filmmakers can only launch their desperately limp plot: The White House turns to these monstrous superheroes to save the planet from evil Gallaxhar (Rainn Wilson), a squidlike creature with four eyes and twice as many legs, and a one-eyed tin robot to do his dirty work for him. Ginormica gets a kick-butt finale, and is a much stronger character -- in any number of ways -- than the movie's president. (In a genuinely witty casting touch he's voiced by Stephen Colbert.) That may be good politics or at least a sound marketing decision from the studio's perspective -- it's been awhile since a family animated feature produced a genuinely strong female character (unless you count "Coraline," which was way too scary for my family) -- but Susan's self-esteem is an awfully long time coming. iReport.com: What do you think of 'Monsters vs. Aliens'? (Bizarrely -- and maybe it's just my imagination -- Gallaxhar bears a passing resemblance to President Obama. I wonder ... would that make Susan/Ginormica a surrogate for Sarah Palin or Hillary Clinton?) Visually, too, "Monsters vs Aliens" is undistinguished, although its shortcomings may be disguised if you seek out the 3-D version. Funny how 3-D movies tend to produce two-dimensional characters, with "Coraline" again the exception to the rule. Jocular and unpretentiously trashy, "Monsters vs. Aliens" should be a lot of fun -- and it is, in places. But the truth is it's as hung up on itself as Susan's preening fiance. Hand on heart, I had a better time at "Space Chimps." "Monsters vs. Aliens" runs 94 minutes and is rated PG. For Entertainment Weekly's take, click here.

Here is a polished, professional, and eloquent version of the review, retaining all original facts, opinions, and references:

***

**(CNN)** — Beware: another bloated, over-produced, high-concept spectacle has escaped the studios at DreamWorks Animation, intent on captivating young audiences. In *Monsters vs. Aliens*, an oversized heroine named Susan—dubbed "Ginormica"—is called upon to save the world. Yet, there is little cause for true alarm. The film is ultimately a relatively harmless, toothless satire packaged with a superficial feminist message and a threadbare plot. 

Such a critique may sound harsh. After all, who wouldn't be entertained by the sight of a 50-foot woman hurtling through San Francisco on improvised roller skates made of automobiles—the ultimate demolition derby? Yet, a moment’s reflection exposes the flaw in the spectacle: roller skates function because of fixed wheels, whereas motorcars would render such momentum impossible. While this might seem overly pedantic, it underscores a key distinction. One would rarely catch Pixar playing so fast and loose with the laws of physics. This disregard for detail typifies the lackadaisical storytelling characteristic of DreamWorks animated features. (Incidentally, the creative talent behind this production includes the directors of *Shrek 2* and *Shark Tale*, alongside the writers of *Kung Fu Panda* and *The Rocker*.) Unfortunately, high-concept premises, top-tier voice talent, and a barrage of pop-culture references cannot substitute for a coherent screenplay.

Our oversized protagonist begins as the ordinary, petite Susan Murphy (voiced by Reese Witherspoon). Moments before she is set to wed the vain, chauvinistic Derek (Paul Rudd), she is struck by a meteorite. Her sudden and dramatic growth spurt spares her from that particular fate worse than death, even if her new companions initially seem little better. Her fellow captives include Dr. Cockroach (Hugh Laurie), a mad scientist who semi-inadvertently mutated into an insect; B.O.B. (Seth Rogen), an amorphous, gelatinous blue blob who functions quite contentedly without a brain; the Missing Link (Will Arnett), a boastful amphibian; and Insectosaurus, a giant dust mite who remains silent simply because he has nothing to say.

Aficionados of classic science fiction will take pleasure in identifying homages to a myriad of cinematic landmarks—including *Close Encounters of the Third Kind*, *Invaders from Mars*, *The Fly*, *The Creature from the Black Lagoon*, *The Blob*, *Mothra*, and *Attack of the 50-Foot Woman*. Viewers will also appreciate a few clever flourishes, such as Kiefer Sutherland’s performance as General W.R. Monger, an obvious homage to George C. Scott in *Dr. Strangelove*.

The difficulty arises once the introductions conclude and the filmmakers must launch their decidedly lackluster narrative. The White House calls upon this misfit cadre of monstrous superheroes to defend the planet against Gallaxhar (Rainn Wilson)—a four-eyed, eight-legged, squid-like alien—and his one-eyed robotic henchman. 

Susan is granted an action-packed climax and proves to be a vastly superior character—in every sense—to the film’s President (humorously voiced by Stephen Colbert). While this framing may represent astute politics or smart studio marketing—given the rarity of genuinely strong female leads in family animation since *Coraline* (which proved far too frightening for my own household)—Susan’s journey toward self-worth is painfully delayed. 

*(iReport.com: What are your thoughts on 'Monsters vs. Aliens'?)*

Peculiarly—though perhaps it is merely my imagination—Gallaxhar bears a passing resemblance to President Obama. One is left to wonder: does Susan/Ginormica serve as a surrogate for Sarah Palin or Hillary Clinton?

Visually, *Monsters vs. Aliens* remains uninspired, though its aesthetic shortcomings may be somewhat masked if viewed in 3-D. Regrettably, 3-D technology frequently yields two-dimensional characters, with *Coraline* remaining the rare exception to the rule. Playful and unpretentiously trashy, *Monsters vs. Aliens* ought to be immensely entertaining—and in certain moments, it is. Yet, much like Susan’s preening ex-fiancé, the film is excessively self-absorbed. Truthfully, I enjoyed *Space Chimps* more.

*Monsters vs. Aliens* has a running time of 94 minutes and is rated PG. For Entertainment Weekly's review, click here.

**Title:** Style Over Substance: How *Monsters vs. Aliens* Exemplifies DreamWorks’ Narrative Shortfalls

During the late 2000s, the battle for computer-animation supremacy was defined by two distinct philosophies: Pixar’s commitment to emotional depth and meticulous world-building, and DreamWorks Animation’s penchant for irreverent, star-powered spectacles. Released in 2009, DreamWorks’ *Monsters vs. Aliens* stands as a quintessential artifact of this era. The film aggressively attempts to construct a high-concept sci-fi comedy by assembling a colorful squad of misfit creatures around a giant heroine. Yet, despite its kinetic energy and star-studded call sheet, the feature ultimately devolves into a bloated, incoherent narrative that highlights DreamWorks' recurring habit of prioritizing flashy gimmicks over genuine storytelling logic.

On paper, the film’s premise boasts undeniable potential. On her wedding day, modest suburbanite Susan Murphy (voiced by Reese Witherspoon) is struck by a meteor full of "quantonium," causing her to grow to a height of fifty feet. Promptly captured by the U.S. government, she is rebranded "Ginormica" and locked away in a secret facility alongside an ensemble of homage-heavy creatures: B.O.B. (Seth Rogen), an indestructible, brainless gelatinous mass; Dr. Cockroach, Ph.D. (Hugh Laurie), a mad scientist turned insect-hybrid; The Missing Link (Will Arnett), an amphibious macho-man; and Insectosaurus, a massive, babyish grub. When an alien overlord named Gallaxhar (Rainn Wilson) invades Earth, the military—led by the bombastic General W.R. Monger (Kiefer Sutherland)—sends the monsters into battle as humanity’s last resort.

To sell this absurd conceit, the studio threw everything at the wall. The film relies heavily on a celebrity voice cast that includes Stephen Colbert as an incompetent U.S. President, leaning into frantic pacing, wall-to-wall pop-culture references, and loud, over-the-top action sequences designed to show off the studio's push into 3D technology. From a destruction-filled brawl on the Golden Gate Bridge to a frantic escape from an alien spaceship, the film moves at a breakneck speed designed to keep the audience too distracted to ask basic narrative questions. 

However, beneath its bright colors and relentless noise, *Monsters vs. Aliens* collapses under its own weight. The film claims to operate as both an affectionate parody of 1950s "B-movie" creature features and a modern tale of female empowerment, but its satire is entirely toothless. Rather than offering sharp commentary on cold-war paranoia, gender roles, or the absurdity of classic sci-fi tropes, the movie settles for low-hanging jokes, lazy slapstick, and surface-level references that age instantly. 

More damning is the film's structural incoherence. Susan’s journey toward self-worth—learning to embrace her new size after being dumped by her self-absorbed news-anchor fiancé—is repeatedly sidelined to make room for chaotic set pieces and non-sequitur gags. The film never establishes clear internal rules for its universe or its characters' powers, leaving emotional arcs feeling unearned and action beats feeling arbitrary. The supporting monsters, while amusing in short bursts, are reduced to static comic relief rather than fully realized characters with distinct motivations.

Ultimately, *Monsters vs. Aliens* serves as a clear case study in the contrasting approaches of animation’s titan studios. Where Pixar spent the same era crafting tight, emotionally resonant, and logically sound masterpieces like *WALL-E* and *Up*—films where visual spectacle serves the narrative—DreamWorks crafted a film where narrative is merely a thin clothesline used to hang visual stunts and celebrity riffs. While *Monsters vs. Aliens* offers a brief, sugar-rush hit of sensory entertainment, its lack of storytelling discipline leaves it a forgettable entry in animated cinema, proving that even the most ambitious concepts will fail to make a lasting impact without a solid script to anchor them.

counterfactuals.output:
**Review: 'Monsters vs. Aliens' offers big 3D thrills, tiny substance**

**(CNN) —** DreamWorks Animation really wants you to put on the 3D glasses, swallow the overpriced popcorn, and above all, turn off your brain. 

In "Monsters vs. Aliens," the studio has constructed a film that is technically state-of-the-art, aggressively fast-paced, and almost entirely devoid of a soul. It’s a movie designed not by storytellers, but by a committee of marketing executives who mistook volume for entertainment.

The premise promises a affectionate homage to 1950s B-movie cinema. On her wedding day, modest California girl Susan Murphy (voiced by Reese Witherspoon) is struck by a meteor full of space gunk. She glows green, grows to 50 feet tall, and is promptly captured by the U.S. government, who rename her "Ginormica." 

She’s tossed into a secret facility alongside a misfit squad of government-inspected freaks: Dr. Cockroach (Hugh Laurie), a mad scientist with an insect head; The Missing Link (Will Arnett), an ego-driven fish-man; B.O.B. (Seth Rogen), a mindless gelatinous blob; and Insectosaurus, a silent, skyscraper-sized grub. 

When a four-eyed alien megalomaniac named Gallaxhar (Rainn Wilson) invades Earth, the military—led by the gun-ho General W.R. Monger (Kiefer Sutherland)—decides the only way to stop an alien threat is to unleash America’s monsters.

On paper, it’s a fun conceit. On screen, it’s a chaotic churn of pop-culture references, sight gags, and sensory overload.

Directors Rob Letterman and Conrad Vernon move the plot at a neck-snapping pace, presumably terrified that if the camera stops moving for more than three seconds, the audience might notice how thin the material is. The film tries desperately to weave in a message of female empowerment—Susan learns she doesn't need her self-absorbed weatherman fiancé (Paul Rudd)—but the self-help subtext feels tacked on, a shiny sticker placed on a product that is mostly about stuff blowing up.

Where "Monsters vs. Aliens" does succeed, briefly, is in its side characters. Seth Rogen’s brainless B.O.B. manages to squeeze genuine laughs out of pure stupidity, and Stephen Colbert turns in a brilliant, brief vocal performance as a clueless, ego-maniacal U.S. President who attempts to communicate with the invading aliens via a synthesizer keyboard. 

Technically, the film is a milestone—it was the first DreamWorks feature shot directly in 3D rather than converted after the fact. The depth of field is impressive, and the Golden Gate Bridge destruction sequence is undeniably cool to look at. 

But spectacle can only carry a movie so far. 

While rival studio Pixar was preparing to release "Up"—a film that famously made audiences weep in its first ten minutes—DreamWorks was still relying on the same tired playbook: celebrity voice casts, needle-drop soundtrack cues, and kinetic violence. 

"Monsters vs. Aliens" is loud, shiny, and superficially diverting for kids who are easily distracted by primary colors. But for anyone looking for depth beyond the stereoscopic 3D, it’s a surprisingly hollow cage match.

**Bottom line:** A visually polished roller-coaster ride that forgets to give you a reason to care about the passengers. 

*“Monsters vs. Aliens” is rated PG for sci-fi action, some crude humor, and brief language. Running time: 94 minutes.*

**Big Monsters, Small Ideas: Why *Monsters vs. Aliens* Chooses Gimmicks Over Grace**

On paper, DreamWorks’ 2009 animated feature *Monsters vs. Aliens* sounds like an absolute blast. It takes the beloved, schlocky tropes of 1950s B-movies—50-foot women, radioactive mutant bugs, gelatinous blobs, and fish-men—and smashes them into a glossy, modern 3D spectacle. But as the film rolls on, it becomes clear that *Monsters vs. Aliens* is less concerned with telling a coherent, emotionally resonant story than it is with showing off its high-concept pitch deck and pelting the audience with rapid-fire pop-culture references. 

It is a film that mistakes noise for energy and sight gags for world-building—a stark reminder of the narrative divide that separated DreamWorks from its arch-rival Pixar during the late 2000s.

The story follows Susan Murphy (voiced by Reese Witherspoon), a normal woman who is hit by a meteor on her wedding day, turns into a 50-foot giant, and is immediately captured by the U.S. government. She is locked away in a secret facility alongside other "monsters"—B.O.B. (Seth Rogen), The Missing Link (Will Arnett), Dr. Cockroach (Hugh Laurie), and Insectosaurus. When an alien overlord named Gallaxhar (Rainn Wilson) invades Earth, the military decides the only way to save the planet is to deploy these freaks of nature.

The premise is undeniably fun, but the movie treats its high concept like a crutch rather than a foundation. Instead of developing its characters beyond their basic archetypes, the screenplay relies heavily on kinetic set-pieces and lazy nostalgia. Rather than building organic humor out of the characters' personalities or situations, the film routinely hits the pause button to insert out-of-place pop-culture riffs. 

When the President of the United States (Stephen Colbert) attempts to communicate with an alien robot, he does so by playing the theme from *Beverly Hills Cop* ("Axel F") on a synthesizer, followed by a quick homage to *Close Encounters of the Third Kind*. It’s a sequence designed to get a cheap chuckle from the adults in the audience, but it comes at the expense of the scene’s dramatic stakes. The film is littered with these moments—nods to *Star Trek*, *The Fly*, and *Mad Magazine*—that constantly break the fourth wall and undermine any sense of immersion.

This is precisely where *Monsters vs. Aliens* fails in comparison to Pixar’s output from the same era. Consider a film like *Monsters, Inc.* or *The Incredibles*. Pixar also dealt in high concepts—monsters scaring children for energy, or a secret society of retired superheroes—but those films established strict internal logic and honored it. In *The Incredibles*, superpowers had real physical and emotional consequences; the world reacted to the heroes in ways that felt grounded and earned. 

*Monsters vs. Aliens*, by contrast, treats logic as an obstacle to be ignored whenever a joke requires it. Susan’s super-strength and size fluctuate wildly depending on what the scene demands. The physics of the destruction—such as the collapse of the Golden Gate Bridge—are played purely for cartoonish slapstick, draining the alien invasion of any real threat. The film demands that we care about Susan’s personal journey of self-actualization (realizing her vain fiancé Derek isn't worth her time), but her emotional arc is treated like a mandatory checklist item crammed between explosions, rather than the heart of the movie. 

Where Pixar uses its high concepts as a lens to explore deeply human truths—grief in *Up*, isolation in *WALL-E*, or parent-child dynamics in *Finding Nemo*—DreamWorks here uses its high concept merely to sell 3D glasses and action figures. The monsters themselves, while voiced by a talented comedic cast, are flat comic-relief machine guns. Seth Rogen’s B.O.B. gets a few laughs, but he isn't a character; he’s a series of brainless-slime gags. 

*Monsters vs. Aliens* isn't an unmitigated disaster; it is briskly paced, visually bright, and occasionally amusing. But it represents a specific era of studio animation that prioritized kinetic distraction over narrative integrity. By choosing surface-level pop-culture references over real heart, and high-concept absurdism over sound internal logic, the film remains a loud, forgettable artifact of its time—a battle where spectacle won, but storytelling undeniably lost.

**Giga-Bores and Sub-Par Sores: Why *Monsters vs. Aliens* Fails to Launch**

**By Arthur Pendelton**  
*March 27, 2009*

If you’ve been to a multiplex anytime in the last six months, you know that Hollywood has decided 3D is once again the savior of cinema. Put on these plastic glasses, they promise, and the movie will leap out and touch you! If only DreamWorks’ latest animated megabudget spectacle, *Monsters vs. Aliens*, offered something worth reaching back for. 

On paper, the film sounds like a cinephile’s cheeky wet dream: a glossy, $175-million love letter to the atomic-era B-movies of the 1950s. Our heroine is Susan Murphy (voiced with crisp, resilient southern charm by Reese Witherspoon), a bride who is struck by a radioactive meteor on her wedding day and sprouts to a staggering 49 feet and 11.5 inches. 

Promptly whisked away by the military, Susan is rebranded "Ginormica" and thrown into a secret containment facility alongside a parade of creature-feature rejects. There’s B.O.B., a gelatinous, brainless blue blob who is essentially *The Blob* if it were voiced by a giggling Seth Rogen; Dr. Cockroach Ph.D., a mad scientist turned insect (*The Fly*, played with manic British glee by Hugh Laurie); The Missing Link, a macho fish-man (*Creature from the Black Lagoon*, voiced by Will Arnett); and Insectosaurus, a silk-spewing larva the size of a skyscraper (*Mothra*, minus the character development).

When a megascopic alien dictator named Gallaxhar (Rainn Wilson) invades Earth, the government—led by Kiefer Sutherland’s gravelly, bombastic General W.R. Monger—decides to fight fire with freaks. 

To be fair, the film’s first act occasionally sparkles with a sharp satirical edge. The highlight of the entire affair is undoubtedly Stephen Colbert as President Hathaway. Colbert essentially ports over his faux-pundit persona to the Oval Office, delivering a pitch-perfect scene where he attempts to make "first contact" with an alien robot by playing Axel F on a Roland synthesizer, before inevitably hovering his hand over the big red button marked "NUCLEAR MISSLE" (right next to "CAFFEINE FREE COKE"). It is a fleeting, brilliant flash of real comedy.

Unfortunately, once the movie finishes winking at film buffs, it falls into the weary DreamWorks routine: loud set-pieces, frantic pacing, and a barrage of pop-culture punchlines designed to distract you from the utter emptiness of it all. Spotting the homage becomes a tedious game of spot-the-reference. Oh look, it’s *The Day the Earth Stood Still*! Ah, a nod to *Attack of the 50 Foot Woman*! But a reference is not a joke, and a nostalgia trip is not a substitute for a soul. 3D glasses can make objects pop off the screen, but they can’t add depth to a paper-thin script.

Where Pixar treats its homage with reverent storytelling, *Monsters vs. Aliens* treats its monsters like action figures being slammed together by an overstimulated eight-year-old. It’s loud, it’s shiny, and by the time Susan is roller-skating through San Francisco using two city buses as footwear, it is overwhelmingly boring. 

By the third act, as giant robots smash into bridges and explosions blind you through your stereoscopic lenses, a terrifying realization washes over you. Last year, Vanguard Animation dumped a cheap, universally reviled CGI movie into theaters about primates in anti-gravity suits. It was called *Space Chimps*. It was widely considered the absolute floor of modern computer animation. 

And yet, heaven help me, *Space Chimps* was more entertaining than this. 

At least *Space Chimps* had the decency to be brief, unpretentious trash. *Monsters vs. Aliens* is trash dressed up in IMAX 3D, demanding your awe while delivering relentless, mechanical noise. I’d rather be launched into deep space with a trio of unfunny simians than spend another ninety minutes chained to these lifeless, corporate monsters.

**Grade: C-**

**REVIEW: 'Monsters vs. Aliens' delivers high-flying 3-D fun, low-altitude script**

**LOS ANGELES (CNN)** -- If you’re a fan of 1950s sci-fi B-movies, 21st-century computer animation, or simply watching giant things smash into other giant things, DreamWorks Animation has a proposition for you: *Monsters vs. Aliens*. 

The latest digital concoction to hit the big screen isn't just a movie; it's a nostalgic, pop-culture-infused spectacle designed to pull you out of your seat and slap a pair of plastic 3-D glasses right onto your face. And while it doesn't quite reach the emotional heights of Pixar’s best work, it succeeds in being a fast-paced, laugh-out-loud summer blockbuster arriving right in the middle of spring.

The story kicks off on what should be the happiest day of Susan Murphy’s life. Susan (voiced with earnest charm by Reese Witherspoon) is an unassuming Modesto girl about to marry a self-absorbed local TV weatherman (Paul Rudd). But fate—and a glowing green meteor—intervenes. Struck by space dust on her wedding day, Susan absorbs the cosmic energy and grows to a whopping 49 feet, 11 inches tall. 

Promptly captured by the U.S. government, she is renamed "Ginormica" and whisked away to a secret subterranean facility. There, she meets her fellow inmates: Dr. Cockroach, Ph.D. (Hugh Laurie), a mad scientist with a roach head; The Missing Link (Will Arnett), an amphibious macho man fresh out of the ice age; B.O.B. (Seth Rogen), a brainless, indestructible gelatinous blob; and Insectosaurus, a 350-foot-tall grub. 

When a megalomaniacal alien named Gallaxhar (Rainn Wilson) invades Earth to reclaim the cosmic energy inside Susan, General W.R. Monger (Kiefer Sutherland) convinces the President (a hilarious Stephen Colbert) to unleash the monsters to save the planet.

Co-directors Conrad Vernon and Rob Letterman bring serious animation pedigree to the table. Vernon, who previously helmed the colossal hit *Shrek 2*, knows a thing or two about subverting classic tropes for modern audiences. Meanwhile, Letterman showed his knack for ensemble character comedy with 2004's *Shark Tale*. Together, they keep the pace breakneck and the jokes coming fast—even if the narrative machinery feels a bit by-the-numbers. 

Where the film truly demands attention is in its technical execution. Marketed heavily as an immersive "InTru3D" experience, *Monsters vs. Aliens* is one of the first major animated features shot directly in digital 3-D rather than converted after the fact. 

The payoff is striking. The 3-D visuals aren't just used for cheap gimmicks (though a side character with a paddleball makes a shameless, joyful play for the audience’s faces). Instead, the technology gives the action sequences genuine depth and scale. A centerpiece battle sequence set on the Golden Gate Bridge is breathtakingly realized, offering a sense of gravity and vertigo that standard 2-D simply cannot replicate. 

Voice performances are strong across the board, but Seth Rogen steals the entire film as B.O.B. His improvised riffing provides the movie's biggest belly laughs. Colbert also turns in a brief but brilliant performance as a commander-in-chief who attempts to communicate with alien overlords via an 80s synthesizer synthesizer duel reminiscent of *Close Encounters of the Third Kind*.

Ultimately, *Monsters vs. Aliens* suffers slightly from a script that favors punchlines over heart. Susan’s journey toward self-acceptance and female empowerment is noble, but it occasionally gets drowned out by the noise of collapsing skyscrapers. 

Still, as a love letter to vintage creature features like *The Blob*, *The Fly*, and *Attack of the 50 Foot Woman*, it’s a roaring success. It may not break new ground storytelling-wise, but it sure looks great smashing through it.

**CNN Verdict:** Three out of four stars. A big, broad, eye-popping ride that will keep kids thoroughly entertained and parents chuckling at the sci-fi callbacks.

### **MOVIE SPECS**

* **Studio:** DreamWorks Animation / Paramount Pictures
* **Rating:** PG for sci-fi action, some crude humor and mild language
* **Run Time:** 94 minutes
* **Directors:** Conrad Vernon, Rob Letterman
* **Voice Cast:** Reese Witherspoon, Seth Rogen, Hugh Laurie, Will Arnett, Kiefer Sutherland, Rainn Wilson, Stephen Colbert, Paul Rudd
* **Format:** Available in 2D, 3-D, and IMAX 3-D

Home > Film Reviews > Animated > Monsters vs. Aliens (2009)

FILM REVIEW
Big Monsters, Little Substance: DreamWorks’ 'Monsters vs. Aliens' Stumbles Under the Weight of Its Own Gimmicks

By Arthur Pendelton | Senior Staff Critic
Published: March 27, 2009 | 09:14 AM EST

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
MOVIE INFO:
Title: Monsters vs. Aliens (3D)
Director: Rob Letterman, Conrad Vernon
Starring: Reese Witherspoon, Seth Rogen, Hugh Laurie, Will Arnett, Kiefer Sutherland
Runtime: 94 minutes
Rating: PG
Studio: DreamWorks Animation
Our Score: ★★☆☆☆ (2 out of 5 stars)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

DreamWorks Animation has spent the last decade positioning itself as the cynical, pop-culture-obsessed counterweight to Pixar’s soulful storytelling. With "Monsters vs. Aliens," the studio’s latest 3D digital spectacle, they have achieved a technological milestone—it is their first feature authored directly in 3D. If only the writers had spent half as much time authoring a coherent script.

What should have been a roaring, affection-drenched homage to 1950s sci-fi B-movies instead plays out like a collection of noisy, hastily storyboarded set pieces looking for a plot. The film is plagued by a lackadaisical narrative approach that assumes dazzling computer-generated destruction and a few retro references can substitute for actual storytelling.

The premise is painfully thin: On her wedding day, unassuming Modesto resident Susan Murphy (voiced by Reese Witherspoon) is struck by a radioactive meteorite. She absorbs the cosmic energy "quantonium," grows to fifty feet tall, and is promptly captured by the U.S. government. Rechristened "Ginormica," she is locked away in a secret facility alongside a misfit crew of classic movie-monster stand-ins: the gelatinous B.O.B. (Seth Rogen), the amphibious Missing Link (Will Arnett), the mad scientist Dr. Cockroach (Hugh Laurie), and a oversized grub named Insectosaurus. When a generic alien warlord named Gallaxhar (Rainn Wilson) arrives to invade Earth, President Hathaway (Stephen Colbert) offers the monsters their freedom if they can stop the threat.

And that is quite literally the entire movie.

Once the setup is complete, the screenplay—credited to an alarming five different writers—effectively gives up on character development or narrative momentum. The film moves lethargically from one spectacle to the next: a destructive brawl on the Golden Gate Bridge, a frantic chase through San Francisco, and a chaotic finale aboard the alien mothership. Between these set pieces, the dialogue relies heavily on screaming, sight gags, and pop-culture references that already feel dated on opening weekend. The storytelling is so lazy that Gallaxhar’s motivation for conquering Earth begins and ends with "he is an alien and he is bad."

Most disappointing, however, is the film's cynical attempt to market itself as a modern tale of female empowerment. On paper, Susan’s arc is supposed to be the emotional core of the film: a woman who learns to stop shrinking herself to fit the ambitions of her narcissistic weather-man fiancé, Derek (Paul Rudd), and embrace her own literal and figurative strength.

In execution, this "feminist message" is entirely surface-level, reduced to a hollow studio-exec checklist item. Susan does not gain confidence through agency, internal growth, or meaningful choices; she is simply thrust into situations where being fifty feet tall allows her to punch things. Her character arc is bizarrely passive for a protagonist. She spends the first half of the film whining about wanting her old life back, and her ultimate realization of independence feels tacked-on during a brief, unearned confrontation with her ex-fiancé. The film seems to think that slapping a "girl power" coat of paint on a classic monster trope is enough to pass for progressiveness, ignoring the fact that Susan remains largely a plot device in her own movie. 

The supporting monsters fare no better. While Seth Rogen manages a few chuckle-worthy improvisations as the brainless B.O.B., Hugh Laurie and Will Arnett are given almost nothing to do beyond spouting canned quips during action sequences. The potential for a genuinely heartfelt story about societal outcasts finding family in one another—a theme Pixar mastered years ago—is entirely squandered in favor of paddleball-in-your-face 3D tricks.

Technically, *Monsters vs. Aliens* is bright, colorful, and polished. The rendered environments are detailed, and the 3D depth is admittedly impressive. But behind the shiny, high-tech curtain lies a creatively bankrupt effort. It is a movie that treats its audience like easily distracted children who require a loud noise every thirty seconds to stay engaged. 

For all its giant scale, *Monsters vs. Aliens* is fundamentally small-minded—a film that aims for the stars in visual effects, but lands squarely in the bargain bin of animated storytelling.
